scope: Place as the third P of the marketing mix: the working definition (how and where an offering reaches the customer, also called distribution — OpenStax 1.2, 17.1, and Introduction to Business 11.3; CFI 4 Ps); the marketing channel as the system that makes goods available for purchase (OpenStax 17.1; AMA dictionary); direct versus indirect channels with original examples (OpenStax 17.2); the channel partners named — wholesalers, retailers, distributors, each with a one-line job (OpenStax 17.1); online versus physical channels, including multichannel and omnichannel systems (OpenStax 17.2); distribution intensity — intensive, selective, exclusive (OpenStax 17.3); place and convenience, the right product at the right place at the right time, with an original example (OpenStax 17.1 and 17.3; CFI); and the honest framing that place is the P nobody notices until it fails (OpenStax Introduction to Business 11.3). Out of scope: the marketing mix as a whole (own topic), the customer journey (own topic), and logistics depth (warehousing, transport operations, inventory mechanics — the operations subject owns that depth). No unverifiable statistics; all examples original.

claims.claim: In the marketing mix, place considerations focus on how and where to deliver the product to the consumer most likely to buy it, and distribution describes how a company makes its market offering accessible for purchase.

Place (distribution) strategy is creating the means — the channel — by which a product flows from the producer to the consumer; it includes physical location, inventory and control systems, transportation, supply chain management, and presence on the web.

Place refers to the location of the customers or potential customers, not the location of the company itself; the job is getting the offering from where it is (such as a warehouse) to where the customers are.

A marketing channel is a system of people, organizations, and activities that work together to make goods and services available to consumers to purchase; ownership of the goods or services is transferred from one channel member to the next along the channel.

A distribution channel is the path a product travels from the manufacturer, through any middlemen, to the end user, including all the activities involved in transferring ownership from the point of production to the point of consumption; channel members may be manufacturers, wholesalers, agents, distributors, or retailers.

A direct channel uses no intermediaries — the manufacturer distributes its market offering directly to consumers; an indirect channel uses one or more intermediaries to distribute the offering to consumers.

The major types of intermediaries are agents or brokers, distributors, wholesalers, and retailers: a distributor takes ownership of products and tends to align closely with a manufacturer; a wholesaler buys a variety of products in large quantities and bulk-breaks them into assortments sized for retailers; a retailer takes ownership and focuses on reaching the end user or customer directly.

Intermediaries add value to customers by reducing the number of transactions (without them, customers would have to buy directly from every manufacturer), bulk-breaking large quantities into customer-sized units, and sharing information; a multichannel system is one company using several distribution channels at once, and an omnichannel system blends channels so consumers can buy, receive, and return in a seamless mix (such as buying online and picking up in store).

Distribution intensity comes in three strategies: intensive distribution uses all possible intermediaries so the product is available virtually everywhere; selective distribution uses more than one but fewer than all possible intermediaries; exclusive distribution allows only a limited number of intermediaries, which can reinforce a premium position.

The goal of channel design is to get consumers the right products and services at the right place and at the right time (OpenStax), and the point of managing trade channels is to make the product readily available to the customer at the right time and place (CFI); buyers who value convenience expect outlets close to where they live, work, or shop.

A marketing mix is only as good as its weakest part: an excellent product with a poor distribution system could be doomed to failure, and an excellent product with an excellent distribution system but an inappropriate price is also doomed — place is the element that usually goes unnoticed until it fails.

conflictingEvidence: No conflicting evidence found among the consulted sources. OpenStax 1.2 says place is where the product is purchased and focuses on how and where to deliver the product to the consumer most likely to buy it; OpenStax 17.1 defines distribution as making the market offering accessible for purchase; OpenStax Introduction to Business 11.3 calls place (distribution) strategy the creation of the channel by which a product flows from producer to consumer — the same idea at three levels of detail. CFI's 4 Ps page frames place as where products are made available for sale and stresses availability at the right time and place, consistent with OpenStax. The AMA dictionary's distribution-channel entry (via marketing-dictionary.org) agrees with OpenStax that channel members include wholesalers, agents, distributors, and retailers. OpenStax lists four intermediary types (agents or brokers, distributors, wholesalers, retailers); this lesson names the three in its curriculum core and mentions agents in passing. OpenStax 17.3 is the source for the intensive/selective/exclusive strategies; terminology matches standard textbook usage.
